title: Take up your bed (Luke 5:12–26)
hookLine: a leper touched, and a man let through a roof by friends
carry: we have seen strange things today

cards: Two people today can't get close to Jesus on their own. The first is a man "full of leprosy," as Luke puts it.

In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of skin diseases, and it meant living apart, kept at a distance from family and worship. He falls on his face: "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Not can you.
If you want to. And Jesus "put forth his hand, and touched him." Before the healing, the touch, maybe the first the man had felt in years.
The second person is lying on a mat in a house so crowded no one can get in the door.

teach.b: Jesus is teaching inside, and the room is packed with teachers of the law from Galilee, Judea, even Jerusalem. Some men arrive carrying their paralyzed friend on a bed, and can't get through the crowd.

So they climb onto the roof and, in the King James words, "let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus." Dust falling, tiles lifted, a mat swaying down on ropes into the middle of a lecture.
Then: "And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee." Their faith. The friends'.
The man on the mat may not have said a word.
The teachers ask a serious question, and a fair one from their scriptures: "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?"

Jesus answers by doing the visible thing so they'll believe the invisible one: "Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house." The man stands, picks up the bed that carried him, and walks home praising God.

teach.h: WE HAVE SEEN STRANGE THINGS TO DAY.
teach.b: And the whole room in one line: "We have seen strange things to day." The Greek is paradoxa, things contrary to what anyone expected, where English gets paradox. Christians see in this scene who Jesus is.
Anyone can see in it what good friends are.

how: Many Christians point to the friends on the roof when they pray for others or help someone who can't help themselves, sometimes called carrying someone in prayer.

o: a saying that seems to contradict itself
things beyond all expecting, strange to see
a miracle only the faithful are able to see

games.q: what's inside Luke 5:12–26 — tap the pairs.
p: if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean
who can forgive sins, but God alone?

s: Jesus healed the man with leprosy without touching him
Luke says he put forth his hand and touched him.
Luke says Jesus saw the friends' faith
when he saw their faith, he spoke to the man on the mat.
the English word paradox comes from the Greek in this story
paradoxa: strange things, contrary to expectation.

games.q: you and three friends are carrying a man on a mat. the house is packed and the door is blocked. what do you do?
o: wait outside until the crowd leaves.
climb on the roof and lower him through the tiles.
take him home and try another day.
games.why: they go up on the roof, open the tiles and lower him into the middle of the room, and Jesus sees their faith.

practice: Picture the friends on the roof, lifting tiles, lowering the ropes slowly, and let one person come to mind who can't get where they need to be on their own right now: a ride, a hand with a form, or just carrying for a while because they're too tired to walk.
Ask whether there's a way around the crowd, a call or a door you could open. If you pray, you can carry that person to God in your mind; if you don't, simply carry them in your thoughts.

wordCard.voice: Paradoxa, Luke's Greek word for strange things, beyond all expecting: a paralyzed man's friends lower him through a roof, and he rises, takes up his own bed, and walks home.

orig.note: Greek: strange things, beyond all expecting. the root of the English word paradox.

carryVoice: Your line: we have seen strange things today. Sometimes the strange thing is a friend who won't give up. Day five hundred twenty, done.
